report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Longitudinal research links participants' responses across waves, yet sensitive topics often require anonymity.
Self-generated identification codes (SGICs) reconcile both, but participants may sometimes mistype, skip, or swap code parts.
Most studies handle such mismatches with ad hoc rules of unknown accuracy.
We present a simulation-based workflow and introduce the web app wavelink for choosing a customized matching procedure.

To link waves, researchers must describe their design, SGICs, and expected errors; wavelink then simulates studies with known true links, compares exact, rule-based (tiered), and probabilistic procedures, recommends the procedure that misses the fewest links within a set false-link limit, and exports an R script for linking the researcher's study data.
To illustrate, we report a three-wave school panel of adolescents, for which error-tolerant procedures found 91-92% of true links versus 73% for exact matching.
Simulations across conditions show that code length limits accuracy and that auxiliary variables compensate for short codes.

therefore enable anonymous (strictly speaking, pseudonymous) data collection, which is particularly useful for longitudinal research on sensitive topics or for collecting information from vulnerable populations (Lipp, 2021).

text.text: SGICs are particularly helpful in school-based research with children and adolescents.
In schools, tracking minors across multiple waves is critical for evaluating the impact of educational interventions, policies, and environments (Agley et al., 2021; Brändle & Pläschke, 2024).

text.text: At the same time, research with children and adolescents, especially on sensitive, stigmatized, or illegal behaviors, often requires anonymous data collection to obtain honest responses (Brändle & Pläschke, 2024; COMPASS Study), and adolescents tend to answer sensitive questions more sincerely when they feel that their identity is protected (Ripper et al., 2017).

text.text: Evaluating matching procedures with real data is challenging because it is often unknown which codes truly belong to the same individual.
To address this, we combine a simulationwhere the true links are known, allowing us to identify both missed and false links -with an application to real data.
Specifically, this study proposes a step-by-step workflow that assists researchers in determining which matching procedure is best suited for their study design.

To make this workflow accessible, we introduce the web app wavelink, which guides researchers through this process, determines the best matching procedure through simulation, and provides custom R code to apply this procedure to their own data.
The app is written in R (R Core Team, 2025) with the shiny package (Chang et al., 2026).

text.text: Linking erroneous SGICs is difficult because it is unknown which records belong to the same person.

We therefore propose a workflow in which researchers describe their study design (i.e., number of waves, parts of the SGIC, other variables collected) and let a simulation determine the best linkage procedure for their study.
This procedure can then be applied to the real data based on an estimate of how many correct and false links to expect.

text.text: Ethical approval was obtained from the responsible ethics committee in each country.
Participants were recruited through collaboration with schools, in accordance with regional education administrations.
Parental consent was required for younger adolescents, as stipulated by country-specific regulations.
All participants also provided their additional consent before starting each of the self-administered surveys.
The surveys were filled out on a computer, laptop, or tablet in schools during class.
Data for T1 were collected from November 2025 through early January 2026, data for T2 from mid-January through April 2026, and data for T3 from May through July 2026.
At the start of each wave, participants were asked to create a personal pseudonymized code.
The questions for this code were derived from prior longitudinal studies (Ripper et al., 2017).

The introduction explained to the adolescents that the code was needed to match the survey responses across waves but that it could neither be used to identify them nor would it reveal anything about them or their answers.

To determine the best matching procedure, wavelink opens with a short overview of the workflow and three ways to begin.

Researchers can start from an empty guide and enter their study themselves, load an example study that fills in every step with a complete setup (design and variables of that study, with the default error and missing rates), or load a configuration they saved in an earlier session.
All entries can be changed afterward, and a decision tree in the sidebar shows which steps have been completed and what was entered.

No participant data are uploaded at any point: the app simulates data that imitate the study from the numbers entered, and the R code generated at the end runs locally on the researcher's own computer.

text.text: When attempting to match participants across waves, the study design is crucial.
For example, the more participants drop out or join at later waves, the more records there are that a procedure can link wrongly.
Wave size matters for the same reason: with more records, more pairs of different persons share a code by chance.

Researchers can typically determine these numbers from their field records; retention can be estimated from response counts per class or school, or from an exact-code linkage, which underestimates it slightly.

In wavelink, both retention and new participants must be set for each wave, because for more than two waves, every later wave is compared with all persons seen so far, using each person's best-matching earlier record.
Records that cannot be linked join the list as new persons, so participants who skip a wave can still be found in the next.
To illustrate, the [blinded] example study had three waves with 1,581 participants in the first wave.
We roughly estimated participation from the data and set retention to 65% (Wave 1 to 2) and 59% (Wave 2 to 3).
Of the participants who missed a wave, 21% returned, and new participants accounted for 16% and 7% of the first wave.
The SGIC determines how well participants can be matched.
Each part of the SGIC is specified by type: letters (e.g., an initial), days, months, generic numbers (e.g., a digit of the house number) or categories (e.g., twin status).

The usefulness of each part depends on its distribution (e.g., how common each initial is), its error rate (how often a participant enters a value in a wave that differs from their true one) and its missing rate.
Furthermore, some errors affect several parts at once: a participant may not answer the code at all, enter a completely different code, or swap two parts.
Errors also cluster in careless participants: in surveys with little at stake, about 12% of participants answer carelessly (Ward & Meade, 2023, p. 581).

text.text: However, few researchers know these rates before data are collected.
The web app therefore uses a literature-based default for every rate, which researchers can use as a starting point and/or replace with their own estimates.
Because adolescents and adults may differ in their error rates, each default is set at an average of adolescents and adults.
For the [blinded] example study, the six SGIC parts (see Table 1) were entered as three letters, a day, a month, and twin status as a category with three values.

Besides the SGIC, many surveys ask for other variables that remain stable (e.g., gender, country of birth) or change in a predictable way (e.g., age rises by one per year, grade by one per school year).

Such variables can help in two ways: First, when two records differ in only a few code parts, agreement on these variables makes it more likely that the records belong to the same person; second, they can be used for blocking, which means that only records with the same value (e.g., the same school) are compared.
In wavelink, each variable is described by its type (category, number, or free text), its distribution, and its error and missing rates.
Two features are specific to panel data.
First, numbers such as age or grade level may change between waves, so researchers specify by how much (e.g., by 0 to +1 per wave).

Second, free texts such as a school name may be typed differently in different waves ("Goethe-Gymnasium", "Goethe Gym", "Gg") and are therefore compared by their similarity (Jaro-Winkler; Winkler, 1990): two texts agree if their similarity exceeds a cutoff.

text.text: A matching procedure is a sequence of steps.
Each step can link records that are still unlinked, but it may also add false links.
We distinguish two kinds of steps.

Rule-based steps link a pair of records if their codes are identical (exact), differ in at most k parts, agree after swapping two parts, or agree on chosen parts; each rule can additionally require agreement on other variables (e.g., gender).
A rule step accepts a link only if it is unique for both records, so that ambiguous records are left for later steps.
In contrast, a score step, which can only be the last step, weighs agreement on all variables and links the pairs with the highest scores, one-to-one, above a threshold.

Two scores are available in wavelink: a weighted score, in which every agreement and disagreement counts with a weight derived from the error rates and distributions entered in Steps 3 and 4 (the log-likelihood ratio of Fellegi & Sunter, 1969; on dependence between linking variables, see Tromp et al., 2008), and probabilistic linkage, in which these weights are estimated from the data with the EM algorithm (Bauman, 2006).

text.text: Because other variables are often related among different persons (e.g., age and grade), wavelink estimates the EM in two stages: first from code parts alone, which identifies the likely matches, and then the weights of other variables given these matches.
Finally, each procedure can block on a variable.
Which procedures to compare is the researcher's choice.
We recommend always including exact matching as the baseline and a score procedure whenever other variables are available.
For the exact codes first, then codes that differ in one part, then codes with swapped day and month or swapped initials; and (C) probabilistic linkage (EM) on all code parts and other variables.
Each of these procedures can make two kinds of mistakes: First, a missed link may split one participant into two, reducing statistical power.
Second, a false link may merge two participants into one, biasing estimates in data analysis (Zhu et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Second, a false link may merge two participants into one, biasing estimates in data analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Zhu et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Missed links show up as attrition, whereas false links cannot be recognized in the linked data afterward.

Wavelink therefore asks for a limit on the share of false links among all links (by default 0.1%, that is, one false link per 1,000 links) and recommends the procedure that misses the fewest links within this limit.
If no procedure stays within the limit, the app recommends the one with the fewest false links and says so.

Researchers who prefer to weigh both mistakes can instead state how many times worse they consider a false link to be compared to a missed one; across typical designs, a ratio of 20 gives about the same results as the 0.1% limit.
Finally, researchers can state how many uncertain links they can check by hand; the score step then gets a review band, and the app exports these links for manual checking.
For the [blinded] example, we kept the limit of 0.1% and did not plan manual reviews.
The simulation assumes clean data, so researchers need to prepare their data before the recommended procedure is applied.

The app lists the necessary steps, and the generated script repeats them as comments: set codes for "don't know" and "no answer" (e.g., -9) to missing; set fake codes (e.g., the same letter in every part) to missing; remove questionnaires submitted twice within a wave; use the same format in every wave (letters as letters, days 1-31, months 1-12, the same category codes); and use the same column names in every wave.
The script also warns about data that look uncleaned.
For the [blinded] example data, we applied these cleaning steps before linking (Step 9), which resulted in the wave sizes reported above.
For the simulation, wavelink generates artificial studies based on the design, variables and errors entered in Steps 2 to 4.
In each simulated study, a population of participants with true values is drawn; in each wave, every participant enters every variable anew, with errors and missing values as specified.
All procedures are then applied to the observed waves exactly as they would be applied to real data, that is, observed records are compared with observed records.
Because the true links are known within the simulation, the app counts the correct, false and missed links for every procedure and threshold.
For waves of more than about 1,000 records, only pairs that agree on at least half of the code parts are compared to increase efficiency.
Thresholds of score steps are chosen on one half of the simulated studies, and all reported numbers are derived from the other half.

We recommend that researchers report at least three measures from the simulation: (1) the share of true links found (recall), (2) the share of false links among all links, and, for more than two waves, (3) the number of persons found in all waves.
Wavelink additionally reports how robust the results are to error rates that differ from the assumed ones and how many links each step contributes.

text.text: Exact matching (A) made almost no false links (0.5 per study, 0.02%) but missed 685 of about 2,519 true links (recall 72.8%).
The rule-based procedure (B) found 91.0% of the true links, but 1.00% of its links were false, about ten times the default limit; most of them came from the step that allows one code part to differ.
Probabilistic linkage (C, with a tuned threshold of a posterior probability of .90) found the highest number of true links (92.1%) and made 1.2 false links per study, a share of 0.05%.
This is within the default limit of 0.1%, so wavelink recommended probabilistic linkage.

It would also have been recommended with a cost ratio of 20, and under a limit of 1% with a lower threshold (recall 94.7%, 0.86% false links).

The robustness check points the same way: with error rates half as high as assumed, probabilistic linkage made 0.02% false links, and with twice the rates, exact matching found only 58.7% of the true links, while probabilistic linkage still found 87.0% and stayed within the limit (0.08% false links).

Still, its share of false links lies close to the limit: when the simulation was repeated with other random numbers, it ranged from 0.05% to 0.10%, and in one of four repetitions it slightly exceeded the limit, so that exact matching would have been recommended.
In such a close case, researchers should decide on the limit on substantive grounds before looking at the results; we return to this point in the Discussion.

Error rates were half, one, two, or four times the literature defaults.
We varied the wave size (300, 1,500, or 5,000 participants, with gender and age as other variables) and, at 1,500 participants, the other variables (none; gender and age; gender, age, and school).
We compared exact matching, the rule-based tiers, the weighted score, and probabilistic linkage under the limit of 0.1% false links.
The results demonstrate that code length sets the limit: with three parts no procedure holds false links below 0.1%, and with four parts only a few conditions allow it.
Procedures that tolerate typing errors recover far more true links than exact matching.

Several limitations should be noted.
First, the workflow was illustrated with a single example data set, a school-based online panel of adolescents in three European countries comprising three waves of data collection.

Designs that differ from this example (e.g., more waves, longer intervals between waves, other age groups, different cultural backgrounds) may yield different results, and the rules of thumb should therefore be applied with caution outside these simulated conditions.
Second, the validity of the simulation depends on the accuracy of its input parameters.

The default error and missing rates are derived from a small number of studies, conducted predominantly with school-aged or adult samples in different contexts, and studyspecific rates are rarely known prior to data collection.

Although the robustness analysis quantifies the consequences of error rates that are half or twice as high as assumed, it cannot account for error structures that are not represented in the data-generating model.
Third, except for careless responding, errors are modeled as independent of participant characteristics, and the other variables are drawn independently of each other.

In empirical data, however, errors may be concentrated in specific subgroups (e.g., younger participants, participants whose first language differs from the language of the survey, or marginalized groups), and other variables are related among different persons (e.g., age and grade level).
Under such conditions, linkage error is no longer random and may introduce bias beyond that implied by the simulated error rates.

In the example data, a single EM over all variables converged to groups of pupils from the same school cohort instead of matches; wavelink therefore estimates the EM in two stages (Step 5), but other dependencies may remain that the simulation cannot reveal.
text.formatted: In the example data, a single EM over all variables converged to groups of pupils from the same school cohort instead of matches; wavelink therefore estimates the EM in two stages <ref type="bibr">(Step 5)</ref>, but other dependencies may remain that the simulation cannot reveal.

text.text: Fourth, the simulation assumes fully cleaned data and, where manual review is specified, error-free reviewer decisions; the reported performance should therefore be interpreted as an upper bound.
Finally, the inclusion of auxiliary variables improves linkage accuracy but simultaneously increases the distinctiveness of individual records.
This potential increase in re-identification risk needs to be weighed against the anonymity that motivates the use of SGICs, particularly when data and code are shared openly.
Linking anonymous survey waves through self-generated identification codes typically relies on ad hoc tolerance rules with unknown error rates.

This paper replaces such rules with a simulation-based workflow: researchers describe their study, compare matching procedures in simulated studies in which the true links are known, and apply the recommended procedure to their own data with an R script that produces the same links as the simulation.

It also introduces the web app wavelink, which makes this workflow available without programming, and the example study shows that its predictions hold up on real data: the false links estimated for the rule-based procedure closely matched the simulation, and error-tolerant procedures recovered substantially more participants than exact matching.

Moreover, simulated rules of thumb suggest that no matching procedure is universally effective: the best choice depends on code length, wave size, the error rates of the code parts, and the auxiliary variables available beyond the SGIC.
Furthermore, the simulation does not determine how much each type of linkage error costs in a substantive analysis.

False links pose the greater challenge because they cannot be identified systematically, whereas missed links bias estimates only when whatever breaks the link also influences the association between predictor and outcome (Breen & Joo, 2026; Doidge & Harron, 2019; Rubin, 1976).

text.text: In linked hospital records, bias from false matches grew when few records had a true counterpart (38% at a 10% match rate, 8% at 70%), and errors that differed between hospitals or related to the outcome distorted estimates most (Harron et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In linked hospital records, bias from false matches grew when few records had a true counterpart (38% at a 10% match rate, 8% at 70%), and errors that differed between hospitals or related to the outcome distorted estimates most <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Harron et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, extant research still mostly lacks validated thresholds, or at least target ranges, for how many false links a study may tolerate.

The example study shows why this aspect matters: probabilistic linkage was recommended with 1.2 false links per study, against about 2.3 allowed, in exchange for 485 additional true links, but in repeated simulations its share of false links came close to the limit or just above it, which would have reversed the recommendation.

We therefore report the conditions under which procedures perform well and leave the choice of tolerance to researchers, because it depends on their study design and on the specific analyses they plan to perform with the linked data.
For researchers who link waves with SGICs, we recommend five steps.
First, expect linkage error and plan for it.
Linkage error can occur in every study, and it is even more likely with codes generated by adolescents.
Linkage belongs to the measurement model, and its error structure is part of the data-generating process (Doidge & Harron, 2019).
text.formatted: Linkage belongs to the measurement model, and its error structure is part of the data-generating process <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Doidge & Harron, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: It can therefore affect every downstream analysis, not only the sample size.
When planning a longitudinal study and deciding on the components of the SGIC, researchers should therefore also include auxiliary variables that support the linkage.

The most common are stable demographic variables such as gender or country of birth, but variables of other types can help as well, such as the number of siblings (a number) or the name of the school (free text).
Second, identify the conditions that drive linkage error.

These are the expected attrition and retention between waves, because a low share of true matches raises the risk of false links (Harron et al., 2014), and the auxiliary variables, such as gender, age, or school, that can support matching beyond the code (Figure 3).

text.text: Once the waves are linked, comparing linked and unlinked participants may indicate whom the procedure loses (Harron et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Once the waves are linked, comparing linked and unlinked participants may indicate whom the procedure loses <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Harron et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Third, choose the procedure by simulation.

Entering the design, the SGIC, the expected error rates, and the available auxiliary variables into wavelink returns the recall and the share of false links of each procedure, and thus the procedure that best suits the study.
Fourth, run sensitivity analyses.
Estimate the main model under the chosen procedure, repeat it under at least one alternative, such as a stricter or a looser threshold, and compare the estimates.
Stable estimates are robust to the linkage decision; estimates that change show that the decision taken on the linkage procedure matters to result interpretation (Gilbert et al., 2018).

text.text: Fifth, report the linkage transparently.
State the procedure, its expected recall and share of false links, and the outcome of the sensitivity analyses (Gilbert et al., 2018).

text.text: SGICs allow researchers to track individuals across waves in longitudinal research without collecting identifying information.
Linking them, however, involves a trade-off between missed and false links, and methodological guidance on matching procedures that protect data quality is scarce.
Because the true links in real data are unknown, this trade-off has so far been managed with study-specific, ad hoc tolerance rules.
To address these gaps, we developed the web app wavelink, which replaces such ad hoc choices among matching rules with insights from a simulation of the researcher's own study.
It compares matching procedures in simulated studies that match the study design, code, and expected error rates.
It recommends the procedure that misses the fewest links within the researchers' false-link limit and exports R code to apply to the real data, along with a methods paragraph for reporting.
The findings indicate that no single procedure is universally optimal.
Code length sets the limit on accuracy; sample size per wave and error rates further decide which procedure performs best, and the availability of auxiliary variables compensates for short SGICs.
We therefore strongly encourage researchers to treat linkage as part of the study design and the measurement model.

This includes planning the SGIC and auxiliary variables with matching in mind, selecting and justifying a procedure through simulation, and reporting its expected accuracy alongside the substantive results.
